A credential is anything that proves something about you — either who you are or what you are qualified to do.

Think of it this way: when you meet a stranger, they have no reason to trust your claims about yourself. A credential is the evidence you hand them so they don't have to take your word for it.
Two Main Things a Credential Can Prove

1. Your Identity — "This person is who they claim to be."

When you log into a website with a username and password, those are credentials. They prove to the system that you are genuinely you, and not someone pretending to be you.

A passport works the same way in real life. It is a credential that proves your identity to a border officer.

2. Your Qualifications — "This person has the right knowledge, training, or authority."

A doctor's medical degree is a credential. It proves that the person has gone through the required education to practice medicine. A driver's licence is a credential — it proves the government has tested you and found you fit to drive.

You will often see this word in the plural — credentials — and this is actually the more common form in everyday use.

When someone asks, "What are your credentials?" they are asking: "What evidence do you have that you are qualified for this?"

For example:

  • A patient might ask a new doctor, "What are your credentials?" meaning: Where did you train? Are you licensed?
  • A hiring manager reviewing a CV is reviewing a candidate's credentials.
  • When you type a password to unlock your phone, you are entering your credentials.

Using the singular ("a credential") typically refers to one specific item of proof — "A degree is a valuable credential." The plural refers to the whole collection of proof a person holds.

In technology and computing, the word has a very specific and widely used meaning: a credential is a username-and-password pair (or similar secret) that proves your identity to a system.

When you sign into Gmail, your email address and password are your credentials. When a developer connects a software application to a database, the application uses credentials (a key, a secret token, or a password) to prove to the database that it is authorised to access it.

In this digital sense, credentials are almost always kept private and secret, because if someone else gets your credentials, they can impersonate you.

Notice that a credential is not the thing itself — it is the proof of the thing.

You are a doctor. That is the fact. Your medical licence is the credential — the document that proves the fact to others who have no way of knowing it otherwise.

You are a student at a university. That is the fact. Your student ID card is the credential.

You are the rightful owner of a bank account. That is the fact. Your PIN number is the credential.

This is why credentials matter so much: the world is full of people who claim things about themselves. Credentials are what separate verified claims from unverified ones.

Not every document or piece of information is a credential. For something to qualify as a credential, it needs to have these features:

  • It is issued or recognised by a trusted authority — a government, a university, a professional body, a company, or a system.
  • It represents a judgement or verification — someone checked, tested, or confirmed something before issuing it.
  • It is presented to someone else who then uses it to make a decision — to let you in, to trust you, to hire you, to give you access.

A random piece of paper you wrote yourself claiming you are a doctor is not a credential. A medical degree issued by a university after years of study is a credential, because a trusted authority (the university) verified your qualifications and stamped their approval on it.

The word appears in many different contexts, but the meaning is always rooted in the same idea:

  • In education: Degrees, diplomas, and certificates are credentials. They prove that you completed a course of study.
  • In professional life: Licences, certifications, and accreditations are credentials. A Chartered Accountant's certification, a lawyer's bar licence, a pilot's flying licence — all credentials.
  • In government and law: A diplomat carries credentials — official documents from their own government that prove they are authorised to represent that country.
  • In journalism: A press credential (often called a press pass) is a document that proves a journalist is recognised and authorised to cover an event.
  • In technology: Usernames, passwords, API keys, security tokens, and digital certificates are all credentials.
  • In everyday speech: When you say someone "has the credentials" for a job, you mean they have the education, experience, and certifications that demonstrate they can do the work.

• "Check someone's credentials" — Verify whether they are truly qualified or authorised.
  • "Present your credentials" — Show proof of your identity or qualifications.
  • "Strong credentials" — Impressive or highly verified qualifications.
  • "Questionable credentials" — Qualifications that are doubtful, fake, or unverified.
  • "Credential theft" — In cybersecurity, this means stealing someone's username and password to impersonate them.
  • "Credentialed professional" — A professional who holds official, recognised certifications or licences in their field.
A credential is a piece of verified proof — issued by a trusted authority — that confirms either who you are or that you are qualified to do something.
